requirement: The `habeas-requirements` skill MUST direct agents, when a change adds, alters, or removes no end-user-observable behavior, to tell the user that no requirement is needed, and when an existing requirement already specifies the behavior the change produces, to tell the user which requirement covers it; in either case it MUST direct them to proceed to implementation without drafting.
rationale:
structural: `requirements.cli.requirements_review_skill.no_change` states only what the `habeas-requirements` skill must tell agents to do. When a change adds, alters, or removes no end-user-observable behavior, agents tell the user no requirement is needed. When an existing requirement already covers the behavior, agents tell the user which one. In both cases they proceed to implementation without drafting. Nothing in the text prescribes a library, algorithm, signature, type, field, or delegation through a named interface.

I checked whether any clause was structural. The only candidate is the reference to "the `habeas-requirements` skill". That names the artifact whose content is constrained. It doesn't dictate how the artifact is built. Any wording, ordering, or section layout of the skill that gives the same directions satisfies the text, so layout is discretionary. The text's obligations concern what the skill's instructions say, and a reviewer judges that from the skill's content. That is observable behavior, not structure.

The supplied root `assets/skills/habeas-requirements/SKILL.md` is the skill document itself. It is already linked to the requirement as an implementation. No structural obligation needs further implementation evidence, so no marker is missing. I did not judge whether the skill's wording is adequate, because that is a behavioral matter outside this criterion.

behavioral: The requirement sets three obligations for the `habeas-requirements` skill. The first is to direct agents to tell the user no requirement is needed when a change adds, alters, or removes no end-user-observable behavior. The second is to direct them to tell the user which requirement covers the behavior when an existing requirement already specifies it. The third is to direct them to proceed to implementation without drafting in either case.

`tests/authoring_cli.rs#fn[the_requirements_skill_skips_drafting_when_no_requirement_changes]` uses `step(SKILL, 1)` to read step 1 of the `habeas-requirements` skill. Through `assert_text`, it asserts that step 1 contains these phrases:
- "If the change adds, alters, or removes no observable behavior". This covers the no-behavior-change case.
- "or an existing requirement already specifies it (most bug fixes), tell the user which requirement covers it, or that none is needed, and go to step 6". This covers both user messages and the instruction to jump to step 6.

The test then asserts `step_of(SKILL, "Implement and test") == 6`. That shows "go to step 6" leads to implementation, so the drafting steps are skipped. The test's body is elided in the supplied text. The helpers `step`, `step_of` and `assert_text` do check the skill text's content.

The assertions would fail if the skill dropped either case, dropped the user notification, or pointed to a step other than implementation. I found no further gap.
